what: A WebSocket client keeps one two-way connection to the server open so messages can flow both ways instantly. The browser does not reconnect for you, so your code needs a small state machine with heartbeat, backoff and a way to catch up on missed messages.
like: Like a walkie-talkie channel that stays on: either side can talk at any time, but you have to notice when the line goes silent and call back.
why: Server pushes arrive instantly, with no polling delay
Chat, presence, live prices and collaboration need messages in both directions
A good client survives wifi drops, sleeping laptops and deploys without losing data

steps.d: Open wss:// (the secure form). Send a short-lived token in the first message or the URL, because the browser API cannot set custom headers.
Messages arrive as events. Parse them, validate the type field, and push them into the store that drives the UI.
The browser API only has send() and close(), so the app sends its own small ping and expects a pong. No pong in time means the link is dead, close it.
On close, wait with exponential backoff plus jitter, then reconnect. Fresh state per attempt; stop on codes that mean do not retry, such as a policy violation.
After reconnecting, send the last seen message id so the server replays the gap (or refetch a snapshot), then flush the outbox.

numbers.l: maximum payload of a WebSocket control frame such as Ping or Pong
the close code a client reports when the connection ended without a Close frame (abnormal drop)

choices.d: Use WebSocket when both sides send often (chat, collaboration). Use SSE when only the server pushes, and polling when updates are rare.
Browser code cannot send protocol ping frames, so send an app-level ping message. A server that sends Ping frames gets a Pong back automatically, per RFC 6455.
Keep a sequence number or last event id, and ask the server to replay from it. If the gap is too large, refetch a full snapshot.
The classic API has none, so a slow tab can pile up messages. Watch bufferedAmount when sending and batch or drop on receive. WebSocketStream has backpressure but is experimental.

instead.why: If only the server pushes, SSE is simpler and reconnects by itself
If updates are rare or you need the simplest thing that works through any proxy

breaks.d: The network drops silently and the socket never fires close.
breaks.see: UI looks connected but nothing updates
breaks.fix: App-level heartbeat with a timeout, then close and reconnect

breaks.d: A deploy drops every client at once and all reconnect at the same moment.
breaks.see: Server overload right after a restart
breaks.fix: Exponential backoff with random jitter and a maximum delay

breaks.d: Events sent while the client was offline are gone.
breaks.see: Chat gaps or stale prices after a reconnect
breaks.fix: Resume from the last seen id, or refetch a snapshot, then apply live events

say: I wrap the socket in a small state machine - connecting, open, closing, closed - and the browser never reconnects for me, so I add backoff with jitter.
Because the browser API cannot send ping frames, I run an application-level heartbeat and treat a missing pong as a dead connection.
After every reconnect I resume from the last event id or refetch a snapshot, so no message is lost, and I buffer outgoing messages while closed.

followups.q: How do you authenticate a WebSocket?
followups.a: The browser API cannot set headers, so use a short-lived ticket or token in the first message or URL, validated by the server, and use wss:// only.

followups.q: When would you pick SSE instead?
followups.a: When data only flows from server to client, such as notifications or token streams. SSE reconnects automatically and works over plain HTTP.

followups.q: What does close code 1006 tell you?
followups.a: The connection dropped with no Close frame, so it was abnormal, for example a network failure. Reconnect with backoff.

today: Most apps still use the classic WebSocket API plus their own reconnect and heartbeat logic or a wrapper library. WebSocketStream adds streams and automatic backpressure, but MDN marks it experimental and not part of any specification.

check.q: The browser WebSocket drops with no Close frame. What code do you see?
check.why: 1006 is how an abnormal closure with no Close frame is reported.

check.q: Does the browser WebSocket reconnect automatically?
check.why: Unlike EventSource, WebSocket has no built-in reconnect.

check.q: 100 clients lose the connection in a deploy. Best reconnect plan?
d: Wait for the user to refresh
check.why: Jitter spreads the reconnects so the server is not hit all at once.
